## M4-E01

**A view that hides the joins** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L255-278](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I'll say create a view and call it longlist”*, [lecture4 L77-80](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“a virtual table”*

```sql
CREATE VIEW "longlist" AS
SELECT "name", "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id";
```

**Why:** The view stores the *query*, not a copy of the rows, so it costs almost no disk space and is always up to date.

## M4-E03

**The average_book_ratings view** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L471-495](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“create a view called maybe average book ratings”*, [lecture4 L514-526](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“Every time I query this view, I'll rerun essentially that query from before.”*

```sql
CREATE VIEW "average_book_ratings" AS
SELECT "book_id", "title", "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "ratings"
JOIN "books" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
GROUP BY "book_id";
```

**Why:** The probe adds two new 5-star ratings to book 1 after the view exists. The view shows the new average immediately, with no refresh.

## M4-E04

**A temporary view built on a view** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L588-612](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I'll say create a temporary view.”*

```sql
CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW "average_ratings_by_year" AS
SELECT "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "average_book_ratings"
GROUP BY "year";
```

**Why:** A TEMPORARY view lives in the `temp` schema and disappears when the connection closes (`.quit`), which suits a one-day analysis.
The ratings are synthetic but engineered to the lecture's results, so you should see the lecture's numbers: 2018 3.75, 2019 3.64, 2021 3.69, 2022 3.87, 2023 3.78 (L581-586).

## M4-E05

**The same analysis with a CTE** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L633-648](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“a CTE exists for a single query”*, [lecture4 L664-696](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I'll use a CTE.”*

```sql
WITH "average_book_ratings" AS (
    SELECT "book_id", "title", "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
    FROM "ratings"
    JOIN "books" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
    GROUP BY "book_id"
)
SELECT "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "average_book_ratings"
GROUP BY "year";
```

**Why:** Lifetimes: a view lasts forever, a temporary view lasts for one connection, and a CTE lasts for one query.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| year | rating |
|---|---|
| 2018 | 3.75 |
| 2019 | 3.64 |
| 2020 | 3.93 |
| 2021 | 3.69 |
| 2022 | 3.87 |
| 2023 | 3.78 |

</details>

## M4-E07

**Try to update a view** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L827-838](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“cannot modify 2021 because it is”*

```sql
UPDATE "2021" SET "title" = 'The Minor Detail' WHERE "title" = 'Minor Detail';
```

**Why:** In SQLite a view holds no data of its own, so it cannot be modified directly (MySQL and PostgreSQL allow it for simple views, errata #11).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

The statement must fail with:
```text
cannot modify 2021 because it is a view
```

</details>

## M4-E09

**An anonymized view for analysts** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L916-942](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I'll say quote unquote "anonymous" as this column name called rider.”*, [lecture4 L962-968](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“In SQLite we can't set access controls”*

```sql
CREATE VIEW "analysis" AS
SELECT "id", "origin", "destination", 'anonymous' AS "rider"
FROM "rides";
```

**Why:** In SQLite anyone who can open the file can still run `SELECT * FROM "rides"`. There are no per-user permissions.
MySQL/PostgreSQL fix this with GRANT (M6-E10).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

## M4-E10

**current_collections, a view over soft deletes** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L1065-1077](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“And now I'll see only those items that have not been deleted.”*

```sql
CREATE VIEW "current_collections" AS
SELECT "id", "title", "accession_number", "acquired"
FROM "collections"
WHERE "deleted" = 0;
```

**Why:** Soft-deleting another item (the probe) removes it from the view at once.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

</details>

## M4-E11

**INSTEAD OF DELETE, turning a delete into a soft delete** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L1133-1170](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“where, in this case, the ID column is equal to the old ID”*, [lecture4 L1178-1194](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“So a good way of trying to use triggers here”*

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "delete"
INSTEAD OF DELETE ON "current_collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    UPDATE "collections" SET "deleted" = 1
    WHERE "id" = OLD."id";
END;
```

**Why:** Without `WHERE "id" = OLD."id"` the UPDATE would soft-delete every artwork (L1148-1153, debugging D4-02).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "deleted" FROM "collections"`

| title | deleted |
|---|---|
| Farmers Working at Dawn | 0 |
| Imaginative Landscape | 0 |
| Profusion of Flowers | 0 |
| Spring Outing | 0 |

`SELECT "title" FROM "current_collections"`

| title |
|---|
| Farmers Working at Dawn |
| Imaginative Landscape |
| Profusion of Flowers |
| Spring Outing |

</details>

## M4-E12

**INSTEAD OF INSERT ... WHEN, re-acquiring a deleted item** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L1246-1278](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I'll say create trigger insert when exists.”*, [lecture4 L1311-1330](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I only flipped that deleted value from a 1 back down to a 0.”*

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "insert_when_exists"
INSTEAD OF INSERT ON "current_collections"
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW."accession_number" IN (
    SELECT "accession_number" FROM "collections"
)
BEGIN
    UPDATE "collections" SET "deleted" = 0
    WHERE "accession_number" = NEW."accession_number";
END;
```

**Why:** The accession number is the museum's own unique id, which makes it the right thing to match on (not `id`, which an INSERT doesn't supply).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "id", "title", "deleted" FROM "collections"`

| id | title | deleted |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Farmers Working at Dawn | 0 |
| 2 | Imaginative Landscape | 1 |
| 3 | Profusion of Flowers | 0 |
| 4 | Spring Outing | 0 |

</details>

## M4-E13

**Assigned: INSTEAD OF INSERT for genuinely new items** · SOURCE · explicitly left to the learner in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L1331-1336](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“For now though, we leave all that up to you.”*, [lecture4 L1236-1242](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“In that case, actually inserting a brand new row”*

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "insert_when_new"
INSTEAD OF INSERT ON "current_collections"
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW."accession_number" NOT IN (
    SELECT "accession_number" FROM "collections"
)
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO "collections" ("title", "accession_number", "acquired")
    VALUES (NEW."title", NEW."accession_number", NEW."acquired");
END;
```

**Why:** Two complementary conditional triggers cover both cases. The lecture also suggests a follow-up you can try on your own:
an INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger, for example to fill in the unknown acquired date (L1333-1334).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "accession_number", "deleted" FROM "collections"`

| title | accession_number | deleted |
|---|---|---|
| Farmers Working at Dawn | 11.6152 | 0 |
| Imaginative Landscape | 56.496 | 1 |
| Profusion of Flowers | 56.257 | 0 |
| Spring Outing | 14.76 | 0 |

</details>

## D4-01

**A trailing comma after the CTE** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture4 L644-646](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“Or I could omit the comma”*

Broken version:
```sql
WITH "average_book_ratings" AS (
    SELECT "book_id", "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
    FROM "ratings" JOIN "books" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
    GROUP BY "book_id"
),
SELECT "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "average_book_ratings" GROUP BY "year";
```

Fixed:
```sql
WITH "average_book_ratings" AS (
    SELECT "book_id", "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
    FROM "ratings" JOIN "books" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
    GROUP BY "book_id"
)
SELECT "year", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "average_book_ratings" GROUP BY "year";
```

**Diagnosis (syntax):** Several CTEs are separated by commas. The last one is followed directly by the main query.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| year | rating |
|---|---|
| 2018 | 3.75 |
| 2019 | 3.64 |
| 2020 | 3.93 |
| 2021 | 3.69 |
| 2022 | 3.87 |
| 2023 | 3.78 |

</details>

## D4-02

**The soft-delete trigger that hid everything** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L1147-1153](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“with no condition it'll update all the columns here”*

Broken version:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "delete" INSTEAD OF DELETE ON "current_collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    UPDATE "collections" SET "deleted" = 1;
END;
```

Fixed:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "delete" INSTEAD OF DELETE ON "current_collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    UPDATE "collections" SET "deleted" = 1 WHERE "id" = OLD."id";
END;
```

**Diagnosis (trigger):** A missing WHERE inside a trigger is just as dangerous as anywhere else, and harder to spot.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "deleted" FROM "collections"`

| title | deleted |
|---|---|
| Farmers Working at Dawn | 0 |
| Imaginative Landscape | 0 |
| Profusion of Flowers | 0 |
| Spring Outing | 0 |

</details>
